alignment.note: Greek opens with the adversative ἀλλά in initial position, matched by Latin Sed; the Peshitta renders the adversative with the postpositive particle ܕܝܢ, which by Syriac syntax stands in second position rather than clause-initial. The note token (1) is a transliteration gloss of the Greek and carries no independent textual weight.
ἐν / in; the preposition is absorbed into the prefixed ܒ of the Peshitta's ܒܗܢܘܢ rather than written separately.
ἐκείναις ταῖς ἡμέραις / in illis diebus / ܒܗܢܘܢ ܝܘܡܬܐ; the Syriac fuses the preposition, demonstrative pronoun (ܗܢܘܢ) and noun into two tokens but conveys the identical 'in those days.'

Greek ἐκείνην and Latin illam both render the demonstrative 'that' agreeing with 'tribulation'; the Peshitta uses the deictic pronoun ܗܘ ('that/it') in postnominal position, a syntactically distinct but semantically equivalent demonstrative usage characteristic of Syriac.
ὁ ἥλιος / sol / ܫܡܫܐ; Greek carries the article, while Latin omits it and Syriac marks definiteness via the emphatic state ending.
σκοτισθήσεται / contenebrabitur / ܢܚܫܟ; all three render the future passive/intransitive 'will be darkened,' the Syriac using the cognate-Semitic root kh-sh-k (cf. Hebrew חָשַׁךְ).
καί / et; in the Peshitta the conjunction ܘ is prefixed to ܣܗܪܐ ('and the moon').

Greek σελήνη and Latin luna are the ordinary words for 'moon'; the Peshitta uses ܣܗܪܐ from the root s-h-r ('to shine/be bright', cf. Hebrew סַהַר), a poetic-Semitic designation of the moon rather than a direct cognate of the Greek term.
οὐ / non / ܠܐ; the negation precedes the verb in all three traditions.
δώσει / dabit / ܢܬܠ; the Syriac imperfect ܢܬܠ derives from the suppletive verb of giving (root y-h-b), morphologically distinct but semantically identical.
τὸ φέγγος αὐτῆς / splendorem suum / ܢܘܗܪܗ ('its light'); the Syriac collapses noun and possessive suffix into the single form ܢܘܗܪܗ from root n-h-r ('to shine').

The Clementine Vulgate marks the clause-end with a colon to bind this verse to the continuing apocalyptic enumeration; the Greek closes with a comma and the Peshitta supplies no terminal punctuation, a purely editorial difference.
